title: 0/1 Knapsack Problem
description: Learn how Dynamic Programming solves constrained optimization problems by maximizing value while respecting limited capacity constraints.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The 0/1 Knapsack Problem is one of the most famous applications of Dynamic Programming. The problem focuses on optimal selection under constraints. Suppose a bag has a limited carrying capacity. You are given several items, each with a weight and a value. The objective is to maximize total value without exceeding the bag's capacity. Each item can only be selected once, which is why the problem is called 0/1 Knapsack.

Think of it like packing a suitcase for a trip. You have limited space measured by weight capacity. Each item has a weight and a value to you, such as usefulness or importance. You want to take the most valuable combination of items that fits within your weight limit. You cannot take fractional items, and you cannot take an item more than once.

This problem is fundamental in computer science because it models many real-world decisions. Choosing investments for a fixed budget, loading cargo onto a ship with weight limits, selecting projects with limited resources, and allocating server capacity all follow the same pattern.

The 0/1 Knapsack Problem demonstrates how Dynamic Programming handles constrained optimization where greedy algorithms fail. It introduces the concept of a 2D DP table and the include-exclude decision that is central to many DP problems.

sections.title: Why the Knapsack Problem Matters
sections.content:
Many real-world systems involve limited resources and optimization constraints. Investment planning requires choosing which stocks to buy with a fixed amount of money. You want to maximize expected return without exceeding your budget. Cargo loading requires selecting which boxes to put on a ship or truck within weight limits to maximize freight value.

Budget optimization in companies requires choosing which projects to fund given a fixed budget. Each project has a cost and expected profit. You want to maximize total profit. Server resource allocation requires assigning tasks to servers with limited CPU and memory capacity to maximize throughput.

Project selection, advertising campaign selection, and even time management follow the same knapsack pattern. You have limited resources like time or money, and you want to maximize value.

The challenge is maximizing benefit while respecting capacity limitations. The Knapsack Problem models this optimization challenge computationally. Understanding knapsack helps you solve many real-world constrained optimization problems.
bullets: Appears in many real-world optimization systems.

sections.title: Problem Setup
sections.content:
Let us define the problem with concrete numbers. You have a knapsack with a weight capacity. You are given several items. Each item has a weight and a value. You want to select a subset of items such that the total weight does not exceed the capacity and the total value is maximized.

Example items: Item A has weight 1 and value 15. Item B has weight 3 and value 20. Item C has weight 4 and value 30. The knapsack capacity is 4.

The possible selections are many. You could take only item C which gives value 30. You could take items A and B together. Their total weight is 1 plus 3 equals 4, which exactly fits. Their total value is 15 plus 20 equals 35, which is better than 30. You could take only item B with value 20, or only item A with value 15.

The optimal solution is to take items A and B with total value 35. This shows that the best combination is not always the single highest value item. You need to consider combinations. The objective is to maximize total value without exceeding the weight limit.

sections.title: Why Greedy Selection Fails
sections.content:
A common beginner instinct is to use a greedy approach. You might think to pick the item with the highest value first, or the item with the best value per weight ratio. Unfortunately, greedy does not work for the 0/1 Knapsack problem.

Suppose we choose item C with weight 4 and value 30 first because it has the highest value. After taking item C, the remaining capacity is 0. You cannot take any other items. The total value is 30.

However, the optimal solution is to take items A and B together. Their total weight is 1 plus 3 equals 4, and total value is 15 plus 20 equals 35. This is better than taking only item C. The greedy choice of the highest value item prevented you from taking the better combination.

Similarly, greedy by value per weight ratio also fails for 0/1 Knapsack. Item C has value per weight 30 divided by 4 equals 7.5, which is actually higher than item A at 15 and item B at about 6.7. Greedy by ratio would also pick item C first and get value 30, missing the optimal 35.

This demonstrates that local greedy decisions may fail globally. Dynamic Programming solves this by efficiently exploring multiple combinations and remembering the best results for each subproblem.

sections.title: Core Dynamic Programming Idea
sections.content:
Dynamic Programming solves the Knapsack problem by storing solutions to smaller capacity problems. Instead of repeatedly recalculating combinations, the algorithm remembers previously computed optimal values. This allows larger optimal solutions to be built from smaller optimal subproblems.

The key insight is to break the problem into smaller subproblems. Consider the first i items and a capacity w. What is the maximum value you can achieve? This subproblem is smaller than the original because you have fewer items to consider.

The DP approach uses two properties. Overlapping subproblems means that the same subproblem appears many times. For example, the best value for capacity 3 using the first 2 items may be needed when computing many larger subproblems. Optimal substructure means that the optimal solution for a larger problem contains optimal solutions for smaller subproblems.

Instead of solving each subproblem from scratch, DP solves each once and stores the answer. When the same subproblem appears again, the algorithm looks up the stored answer instead of recomputing. This transforms exponential brute force into polynomial time.

sections.title: Understanding the DP Matrix
sections.content:
The most important structure in Knapsack Dynamic Programming is the 2D matrix. Rows represent items considered from 0 to n. Columns represent available knapsack capacities from 0 to W. Each matrix cell stores the maximum achievable value for that specific subproblem using the first i items and capacity w.

Row 0 represents considering no items. The maximum value for any capacity with no items is 0. Column 0 represents capacity 0. The maximum value with zero capacity is 0 regardless of items because nothing fits.

As you fill the matrix row by row, you introduce one new item at a time. When you add a new item, you decide whether including it gives a better value than excluding it. The matrix gradually fills using previous optimal values from the row above.

The final answer is in the bottom right corner. That is row n, column W. This cell represents the maximum value achievable using all n items with the full capacity W. The DP matrix transforms recursive optimization into structured table-based computation. Each cell depends only on previously computed cells, so you can fill it iteratively.

sections.title: DP Matrix Visualization
sections.content:
Suppose the capacity is 4 and we have three items. The DP table has 4 rows for items 0 to 3 and 5 columns for capacities 0 to 4. Row 0 is all zeros because with no items, the maximum value is always 0. Column 0 is all zeros because with zero capacity, no items can fit.

When processing item A with weight 1 and value 15, for each capacity from 1 to 4, you can either take the item or not. At capacity 1, you can take it and get value 15. At capacity 2, you can still only take it once, so value 15. At capacities 3 and 4, same value 15.

When processing item B with weight 3 and value 20, at capacity 3, you compare excluding it which gives 15 from the previous row, or including it which gives 20 plus the best value from capacity 0. 20 plus 0 equals 20, so you take 20. At capacity 4, excluding gives 15, including gives 20 plus best from capacity 1 which is 15, total 35. So you take 35.

When processing item C with weight 4 and value 30, at capacity 4, excluding gives 35 from the previous row, including gives 30 plus best from capacity 0 which is 0, total 30. So you keep 35. The final answer is 35, which comes from taking items A and B.

sections.title: Decision-Making Per DP Cell
sections.content:
At every matrix cell, the algorithm decides whether to include or exclude the current item. This decision is made for each item i and each capacity w.

Option 1 is to exclude the current item. If you do not take the item, the best value for capacity w using the first i items is the same as the best value for capacity w using the first i-1 items. This value is stored in the cell directly above the current cell, which is dp[i-1][w].

Option 2 is to include the current item. You can only include it if its weight is less than or equal to the current capacity w. If you include it, you add the item's value to the best value you can get from the remaining capacity, which is w minus the item's weight, using the first i-1 items. This value is value[i] plus dp[i-1][w minus weight[i]].

The algorithm selects the larger result between these two choices. The recurrence relation is dp[i][w] equals the maximum of dp[i-1][w] and value[i] plus dp[i-1][w minus weight[i]] when weight[i] is less than or equal to w. If the item does not fit, you simply copy the value from above. This include-exclude decision is the heart of the Knapsack DP solution.

sections.title: Knapsack Recurrence Relation
sections.content:
The mathematical core of Knapsack Dynamic Programming is the recurrence relation. It defines how to compute each cell in the DP table from previously computed cells.

The recurrence is dp[i][w] equals the maximum of two options. The first option is dp[i-1][w], which means you exclude the current item. The second option is value[i] plus dp[i-1][w minus weight[i]], which means you include the current item. This second option is only available if weight[i] is less than or equal to w.

If the item weight is greater than the current capacity, you cannot include it. In that case, dp[i][w] simply equals dp[i-1][w]. You have no choice but to exclude it.

This recurrence drives the optimization process by comparing inclusion and exclusion choices at every step. It builds the optimal solution for larger capacities from optimal solutions for smaller capacities.

The base cases are simple. dp[0][w] equals 0 for all w because with no items, you get zero value. dp[i][0] equals 0 for all i because with zero capacity, you cannot fit any items. These base cases fill the first row and first column of the DP table.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Let us walk through the complete example step by step. Items are A: weight 1 value 15, B: weight 3 value 20, C: weight 4 value 30. Capacity is 4.

Initialize the DP table. Row 0 is all zeros for capacities 0 to 4. Column 0 is all zeros for items 0 to 3.

Process item A with weight 1 value 15. For w equals 0, dp[1][0] equals 0. For w equals 1, include gives 15 plus dp[0][0] equals 15, exclude gives 0, so take 15. For w equals 2, include gives 15 plus dp[0][1] equals 15, exclude gives 0, take 15. For w equals 3 and 4, similarly take 15.

Process item B with weight 3 value 20. For w equals 0, dp[2][0] equals 0. For w equals 1 and 2, include not possible because weight 3 is greater than w, so copy from above. For w equals 3, include gives 20 plus dp[1][0] equals 20, exclude gives 15, so take 20. For w equals 4, include gives 20 plus dp[1][1] equals 20 plus 15 equals 35, exclude gives 15, so take 35.

Process item C with weight 4 value 30. For w equals 0 to 3, include not possible, so copy from above. For w equals 4, include gives 30 plus dp[2][0] equals 30, exclude gives 35, so keep 35.

The final answer is 35. To find which items were selected, trace back from dp[3][4]. Since dp[3][4] equals dp[2][4] which is 35, item C was not taken. Since dp[2][4] came from including item B, item B was taken. Then subtract weight of B, go to dp[1][1]. Since dp[1][1] came from including item A, item A was taken. The selected items are A and B.

sections.title: Knapsack Pseudocode Pattern
sections.content:
The algorithm processes every item and every capacity using nested loops. The outer loop iterates over items from 1 to n. The inner loop iterates over capacities from 0 to W.

For each cell, check if the current item weight fits within the current capacity. If the weight is less than or equal to w, then compute the value if you include the item. This is item value plus dp[i-1][w minus weight]. Also get the value if you exclude the item, which is dp[i-1][w]. Then take the maximum of these two and store it in dp[i][w].

If the item weight is greater than the current capacity, you cannot include it. In that case, simply copy the value from the row above, which is dp[i-1][w].

After filling the entire table, the answer is dp[n][W], which is the bottom right cell. To recover which items were selected, you can trace back from the bottom right corner. If dp[i][w] equals dp[i-1][w], the item was not taken. Move up to the previous row. If dp[i][w] equals value[i] plus dp[i-1][w minus weight[i]], the item was taken. Record it, subtract its weight from the current capacity, and move up to the previous row.

This repeated matrix transition is the heart of Knapsack Dynamic Programming.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content:
Knapsack implementations commonly use a 2D Dynamic Programming matrix to store optimal intermediate results. The code follows the recurrence relation directly.

First, create a dp matrix of size n+1 rows and capacity+1 columns, initialized to zero. Row 0 and column 0 are already zero. Then loop i from 1 to n, where i represents the first i items. Loop w from 0 to capacity, where w represents the current capacity limit.

Inside the loops, check if the current item's weight is less than or equal to w. The item index is i-1 because the list is zero-indexed. If it fits, compute include as values[i-1] plus dp[i-1][w minus weights[i-1]]. Compute exclude as dp[i-1][w]. Set dp[i][w] to the maximum of include and exclude.

If the item weight is greater than w, it does not fit. Simply set dp[i][w] to dp[i-1][w].

After the loops complete, the answer is dp[n][capacity]. This is the maximum value achievable. The space complexity can be optimized to O(capacity) by using only two rows because each row only depends on the previous row. However, the 2D version is easier to understand and allows item tracing.

The examples below show the complete implementation, a simple comparison of include versus exclude, and how to create an empty DP matrix.

codeSnippets.title: 0/1 Knapsack implementation
codeSnippets.code:
weights = [1, 3, 4]
values = [15, 20, 30]
capacity = 4
n = len(weights)

dp = [[0 for _ in range(capacity + 1)]
for _ in range(n + 1)]

for i in range(1, n + 1):
    for w in range(capacity + 1):
        if weights[i - 1] <= w:
            include = values[i - 1] + \
            dp[i - 1][w - weights[i - 1]]

            exclude = dp[i - 1][w]

            dp[i][w] = max(include, exclude)
        else:
            dp[i][w] = dp[i - 1][w]

print(dp[n][capacity])

codeSnippets.title: Create an empty DP matrix
codeSnippets.code:
rows = 4
cols = 5

dp = [[0 for _ in range(cols)]
for _ in range(rows)]

for row in dp:
    print(row)

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
The algorithm fills every DP matrix cell once. If there are n items and capacity W, the matrix contains n times W subproblems. Each cell requires constant time to compute, so the total time complexity is O(n times W).

The space complexity is O(n times W) for the full 2D DP table. This can be optimized to O(W) by using only two rows because each row only depends on the previous row. You only need to keep the current row and the previous row. Some implementations use a 1D array that is updated from right to left to avoid overwriting values needed later.

However, the 2D version is easier to understand for learning. For small capacities, the memory usage is acceptable. For very large capacities, the space-optimized version is necessary.

Without Dynamic Programming, the brute force solution would try all 2 to the power of n subsets. For n=30, that is about 1 billion subsets, which is borderline. For n=40, that is about 1 trillion subsets, which is impossible. Dynamic Programming transforms exponential recursive combination search into structured polynomial-time optimization. sections.title: Why Knapsack Uses Dynamic Programming
sections.content:
The Knapsack Problem contains overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure, which are the two key properties for Dynamic Programming.

Overlapping subproblems occur because the same subproblem appears many times. For example, computing the best value for capacity 3 using the first 2 items may be needed when computing many larger subproblems. Without DP, you would recompute it each time.

Optimal substructure means that the optimal solution for a larger problem contains optimal solutions for smaller subproblems. For knapsack, the optimal solution for capacity W using n items either includes item n or not. If it includes item n, then the remaining problem is the optimal solution for capacity W minus weight[n] using n-1 items. If it does not include item n, then it is the optimal solution for capacity W using n-1 items.

Without Dynamic Programming, recursive combinations become exponentially expensive. The naive recursive solution would try including or excluding each item, leading to 2 to the power of n calls. For n=50, that is about 1 quadrillion calls, which is impossible.

DP avoids repeated computation by storing optimal intermediate results. This transforms impractical brute-force search into efficient optimization. The DP solution runs in O(n times W) time, which is much faster than exponential for reasonable capacities.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
Knapsack optimization appears in many real-world systems. Cargo loading requires selecting which boxes to put on a ship or truck within weight limits to maximize freight value. Investment planning requires choosing which stocks to buy with a fixed amount of money to maximize expected return.

Cloud resource allocation requires assigning virtual machines to physical servers with limited CPU and memory capacity to maximize throughput or minimize cost. Manufacturing systems require selecting which products to produce given limited raw materials and machine time.

Advertisement selection requires choosing which ads to show within a budget to maximize click-through or conversion. Portfolio management requires selecting which investments to hold given a fixed capital limit to maximize return while managing risk.

Project selection in companies requires choosing which projects to fund given a fixed budget. Each project has a cost and expected profit. You want to maximize total profit. Budget optimization, time management, and even holiday packing follow the same knapsack pattern. Many business optimization systems use knapsack-style decision modeling because it is a fundamental constrained optimization problem.

subsections.title: Mistake: Using greedy selection for 0/1 Knapsack
subsections.content: Greedy selection does not always produce optimal answers for 0/1 Knapsack. The counterexample with items of weight 1 value 15, weight 3 value 20, and weight 4 value 30 shows that greedy picks the highest value item and gets 30, but optimal picks the two smaller items and gets 35.

subsections.title: Mistake: Confusing 0/1 Knapsack with Fractional Knapsack
subsections.content: 0/1 Knapsack only allows complete selection or rejection of items. You cannot take part of an item. Fractional Knapsack allows taking fractions of items, and greedy by value per weight ratio actually works for Fractional Knapsack. Do not confuse the two problems.

subsections.title: Mistake: Misunderstanding DP matrix meaning
subsections.content: Each DP cell represents the best achievable value for a specific subproblem using the first i items and capacity w. Row i does not mean that you must use item i. It means you are allowed to use any of the first i items. This is a common source of confusion for beginners.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: The 0/1 Knapsack Problem focuses on optimal selection under constraints.
Each item can either be selected or skipped.
Greedy selection does not always work correctly.
Dynamic Programming stores optimal subproblem solutions.
The DP matrix represents capacities and item decisions.
Knapsack optimization demonstrates powerful DP reasoning.
